games.title: MUD
games.note: Written at Essex University on a DEC PDP-10; its name partly honors Dungeon, a version of Zork.

games.title: AberMUD
games.note: Students at Aberystwyth wrote it on a Honeywell mainframe; it spread to universities and inspired TinyMUD, LPMud and DikuMUD.

games.title: DikuMUD
games.note: Five Copenhagen students wrote it in 1990–91; its classes, levels and monster grinding shaped later MMOs.

games.title: Habitat
games.note: Players appeared on screen as 'avatars' in a shared online town run over the Quantum Link service.

games.title: Meridian 59
games.note: Often called the first 3D graphical MMORPG; it went online in late 1995 and launched commercially in 1996.

games.title: EverQuest
games.note: Brad McQuaid, Steve Clover and Bill Trost built it from their years playing Diku-style text MUDs.

games.title: EverQuest II
games.note: Set in Norrath 500 years after the first game; it launched about two weeks before World of Warcraft.

games.title: Asheron's Call
games.note: Turbine's first MMO, published by Microsoft; its servers ran from 1999 until early 2017.

games.title: Dungeons & Dragons Online
games.note: An online take on the D&D 3.5 rules in the Eberron setting; it went free-to-play in 2009.

games.title: Dark Age of Camelot
games.note: Built around a three-way war between the realms of Albion, Hibernia and Midgard.

games.title: Warhammer Online: Age of Reckoning
games.note: Introduced 'public quests' that anyone nearby could join; its servers closed in 2013.

games.title: RuneScape
games.note: Andrew Gower began it as DeviousMUD in 1998; it launched as a free Java game playable in a web browser.

games.title: Old School RuneScape
games.note: Restored from an August 2007 backup after a player poll passed 50,000 votes; players still vote on its updates.

games.title: Final Fantasy XI
games.note: Square's first MMO; PlayStation 2 and PC players shared the same servers.

games.title: Star Wars Galaxies
games.note: Led early on by Raph Koster, it let players live as crafters, merchants or entertainers, not just fighters.

games.title: The Lord of the Rings Online
games.note: Its cooking and farming reflect Tolkien's hobbits, and players can perform music together.

games.title: Albion Online
games.note: Made in Berlin; PC and phone players share one world where nearly all gear is crafted by players.

games.title: Lost Ark
games.note: Launched in South Korea in 2019; Amazon Games published it in the West in 2022.

games.title: Star Wars: The Old Republic
games.note: Set 300 years after the Knights of the Old Republic games, with a separate story for each class.

games.title: Shroud of the Avatar: Forsaken Virtues
games.note: Richard Garriott's crowdfunded return to Ultima-style fantasy; his 1977 teletype game DND1 is playable inside it.

games.title: Elite Dangerous
games.note: David Braben's return to Elite, with a full-scale Milky Way of about 400 billion star systems.

games.title: Neverwinter
games.note: A free-to-play online D&D game set in the Forgotten Realms city of Neverwinter.

links.took: Group fantasy adventuring; co-creator Richard Bartle was a D&D player.
links.added: A shared text world where many players explore and fight at once over a network.
links.extra: Bartle says MUD grew mainly from text adventures like Zork; the 'Dungeon' in its name honors Zork, not D&D.

links.took: MUD1's multiplayer text-adventure design; Alan Cox had played MUD1.
links.added: Code that spread to many universities and could be set up anywhere.
links.extra: Wikipedia says its gameplay was heavily influenced by MUD1.

links.took: AberMUD's multiplayer dungeon format, which the Diku team set out to improve.
links.added: D&D-like classes, levels and combat that became a template for later MUDs.
links.extra: Richard Bartle said Diku's authors wanted to create 'a better version of AberMUD'.

links.took: Diku-style classes, levels, group combat and camping monsters for loot.
links.added: A full 3D world, Norrath, where players had to team up to survive.

src.t: Wikipedia: EverQuest (developers cited their years playing Diku-based MUDs)

links.extra: The team played Diku MUDs such as Sojourn and TorilMUD; Verant swore EverQuest used no Diku code.

links.took: Online fantasy play built around skills, combat and a shared world.
links.added: A graphical Britannia for thousands, with housing, crafting and player-run economies.
links.extra: Wikipedia's DikuMUD article lists Ultima Online among MMOs shaped by Diku's gameplay; UO's Raph Koster named DartMUD as his own influence.

links.took: Diku-style classes, levels and grinding monsters for experience.
links.added: Quests to guide players everywhere, plus Warcraft's world and style.
links.extra: Wikipedia's DikuMUD article lists World of Warcraft among MMOs inspired by Diku's gameplay.

links.took: The multi-user dungeon; early on, Meridian 59 was commonly seen as a graphical MUD.
links.added: A first-person 3D view, and guilds that could vote and win guild halls.

links.took: The multi-user dungeon that MUD1 popularized; RuneScape began life as a text MUD.
links.added: Graphics and a free Java client that ran in a web browser.
links.extra: Andrew Gower developed it under the name DeviousMUD from 1998.

links.took: A shared graphical world where many players appear on screen together.
links.added: A full fantasy RPG world for thousands of players, with housing and crafting.
links.extra: Wikipedia's Ultima Online article names Habitat among the earlier online worlds UO followed and outdid.

links.took: Raph Koster, UO's lead designer, and UO-style crafting and player economies.
links.added: Star Wars planets and non-combat careers such as entertainer and architect.

links.took: EverQuest's makers, Verant Interactive, who partnered on development.
links.added: A skill-based sandbox instead of EverQuest's class-and-level design.

links.took: EverQuest-style raiding; Jeff Kaplan said he and fellow leads had extensive EverQuest raiding experience.
links.added: Quests to guide players, softer death penalties and the Warcraft world.
links.extra: Wikipedia: many Blizzard developers were EverQuest fans and wanted to fix what they saw as its weak points.

links.took: The 3D online RPG model; Hironobu Sakaguchi's push for FFXI followed his time playing EverQuest.
links.added: Final Fantasy jobs, story missions and shared servers for PS2 and PC players.

src.t: FFXI creators, 20th anniversary retrospective, PlayStation Blog, 2022

links.took: Norrath and EverQuest's group-based design.
links.added: A new engine and a world set 500 years after the first game.

links.took: WoW's approach to an accessible MMO, which the team studied after the 2010 version failed.
links.added: Final Fantasy's story focus and every job playable on a single character.
links.extra: Yoshida has called WoW a kind of mentor and pointed to the Duty Finder as one borrowed feature.

links.took: Quest-driven MMO play with dungeons and raids, the model WoW popularized.
links.added: Fully voiced class stories with BioWare-style dialogue choices.

src.t: Wikipedia: Star Wars: The Old Republic

links.took: The Old Republic era, Jedi and Sith, and BioWare's dialogue style.
links.added: An online world set 300 years after KOTOR, with eight class stories.

src.t: Wikipedia: Star Wars: The Old Republic

links.took: Space trading and combat; the founders played Elite as kids and wished other ships were real people.
links.added: One persistent galaxy where every ship is a player and losses are permanent.

src.t: Hilmar Pétursson and Reynir Harðarson (CCP), PC Gamer

links.took: A player-driven economy and territory warfare; CEO Stefan Wiezorek named EVE its biggest influence.
links.added: A fantasy setting playable on both PC and phones.

links.took: The old-school sandbox MMO; the studio says its roots are 'very obviously inspired' by Ultima Online.
links.added: Gear that decides your role, and a top-down view that also works on phones.

links.took: Large-scale guild warfare from the older MMOs the studio names as its roots.
links.added: Territory battles sized for small guilds as well as big ones.

links.took: Matt Firor, a Dark Age of Camelot designer, and its three-faction war over keeps.
links.added: Tamriel's three alliances fighting over Cyrodiil and the Ruby Throne in a huge PvP zone.
links.extra: Firor worked on Dark Age of Camelot and later directed The Elder Scrolls Online at ZeniMax Online.

links.took: Mythic's realm-versus-realm warfare between factions.
links.added: Games Workshop's Warhammer setting and 'public quests' open to anyone nearby.

src.t: Wikipedia: Warhammer Online: Age of Reckoning

links.took: Turbine's experience building and running an MMO since 1999.
links.added: Tolkien's Middle-earth, player music and hobbit pastimes like cooking and farming.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Lord of the Rings Online

links.took: Turbine's MMO technology and team.
links.added: Instanced D&D dungeons full of traps, with a narrator playing Dungeon Master.

links.took: D&D 3.5 rules and the Eberron campaign setting.
links.added: Real-time action combat in a shared online world.

links.took: The Forgotten Realms city of Neverwinter and D&D lore.
links.added: Free-to-play action combat and a tool for player-made quests.

links.took: An August 2007 backup of RuneScape, restored after a player poll.
links.added: New content added only when players vote for it.

links.took: Richard Garriott and Starr Long, and Ultima's virtue-themed fantasy.
links.added: A crowdfunded online RPG that mixes single-player and multiplayer modes.

src.t: Wikipedia: Shroud of the Avatar: Forsaken Virtues

links.took: Free online play in the style of Battle.net; ArenaNet's founders had built Battle.net at Blizzard.
links.added: No subscription fee, instanced missions and a skill deck that works like a card game.
links.extra: Battle.net launched with Diablo in 1996; Wikipedia says Guild Wars' infrastructure drew on its founders' Battle.net work.

links.took: Diablo-style isometric action combat, as critics describe it.
links.added: A huge MMO world with raids, sailing and a long gear grind.
links.extra: Reviews at VG247 and Rock Paper Shotgun called it 'Diablo-like'.

links.took: Frontier's realistic, full-scale galaxy and open-ended trading and fighting.
links.added: A persistent online galaxy shared with other players, with VR support.
